kata.name: Singleton near-floor control - one client, two access paths: the shared-reference equation catches the escaped engine row while the conventional count+identity test catches both (control self-negates)
kata.series_report: docs/ref/pattern-kata-dispositions.md Singleton row (unexpressible: unique element - object identity has no predicate); fixtures/katas/singleton/README.md (pre-registered); beads catherine-r5k.7
kata.series_verdict: pre-registered: on the near-floor instance the conventional count+identity test catches the duplicate row and the accessor disagreement, while the kernel catches only the disagreement; the unique set must be empty and the control self-negates (killed). The duplicate's silence is the cardinality gap, recorded but never counted.

expected.detail: Client row 0's engine accessor names Engine row 1 while its fallback accessor names row 0; the accepted equation engine = fallback emits one executed violation (equation 0, row 0). The scripted conventional arm identifies the same element.

The same fixture carries two Engine rows, but the control schema declares no key, so the kernel emits no witness for the duplicate itself; only the conventional count assertion names it. This is the control's copy of the cardinality gap - recorded, not counted.

comparison.conventional_baseline: scripted conventional singleton test: exactly one Engine row, every client's engine and fallback cells resolve to a declared Engine row and name the same row, and seen equals mode(engine(client)); covers both the clean and the fault fixture

baseline.artifact: prototype/singleton_baseline.py sha256:ff109499c871f2b8361c809daddac175dcac9b805d8227aa938864e8479f5873 (scripted conventional singleton test; executed before the probe arm)

expressibility_gap.invariant: the instance contains exactly one row of the declared singleton object Engine
expressibility_gap.why: no field, parse pass, or finding witness constrains an object's row count: equations are pointwise over rows that already exist, and keys are value-tuple injectivity over a non-empty arrow tuple, so a second Engine row with a distinct value is accepted silently (this control schema declares no key at all)

discrepancies: The conventional arm is strictly stronger than the kernel on the control's duplicate row: the count assertion fires while the kernel has no cardinality witness. That is parity in the baseline's favour, not a probe advantage; the control's verdict is killed either way.
procedure: 1. The law was named before any fixture: exact cardinality / unique element, |rows(Engine)| = 1 with every access path resolving to that row (fixtures/katas/singleton/README.md).
2. The conventional arm (prototype/singleton_baseline.py, sha256 above) ran first: exactly-one row, accessor resolution and row identity, and mode coherence, over the frozen fault set.
3. The probe arm ran the same fixtures through the real CLI: `catherine check --json`; the construction probe is the same binary refusing an unparseable document.

4. Witnesses were mapped to the pre-registered element vocabulary; unique = executed probe elements minus baseline-identified elements. A key collision and a row count resolve to the same element (the duplicate); a construction rejection is recorded, never counted.
5. Verdict follows the recorded rule: empty unique = killed (parity or null); the cardinality half is recorded in expressibility_gap, never invented as a finding.
6. Control gate: unique is empty and the verdict is killed, so the control self-negates.
